paragraphs: Choni the Circle-Drawer. He lived in a town named Maglo: the Arukh of R. Tzemach. In Mishnah 8 of chapter 3 of Taanit (23a), they told Choni the Circle-Drawer to pray for rain. He told them, “Bring in the Passover ovens, so that they do not dissolve.” He prayed, but rain did not fall. He drew a circle, stood inside it, and said, “Master of the universe, Your children have turned to me because I am like a member of Your household. I swear by Your great name that I will not move from here until You have mercy on Your children.” Rain began to drip. He said, “That is not what I asked for, but rain for cisterns, etc.” It began to fall violently. He said, “That is not what I asked for, but rain of favor and blessing.” It fell properly, until they left Jerusalem for the Temple Mount, etc. Shimon ben Shetach sent him word: “Were you not Choni, I would decree a ban against you. But what can I do? You importune the Omnipresent and He does your will, like a child who importunes his father.” See there at length, and at 19a. Yuchasin, in its sequence of generations, and Megillat Taanit write that there were three years of drought before Choni the Circle-Drawer prayed; Elyoeini lived then (see there). He was a great Torah scholar, as was his family: his son's son Abba Chilkiyah and his daughter's son Chanan the Hidden were all practiced in miracles [source reads בוסים] and scholars in the Second Temple period; see there. Taanit relates that he slept seventy years. In part 3 of Magen Avot, R. Duran says that this is naturally impossible without [a miracle], because the body’s natural heat would cool. Taanit also says that because they did not treat him with honor in his old age, he requested death for himself: he prayed to die and passed away. Rava said, “This is what people say: either companionship or death.” Yosippon writes that he was killed outside Jerusalem when the Hasmonean kings besieged one another: Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, sons of Alexander son of Hyrcanus I. Shalshelet HaKabbalah likewise writes this (25b), but at 33b writes that he lived in the days of Resh Lakish. It also writes, in the name of a certain scholar, that he saw in the Zohar that Choni the Circle-Drawer was R. Pinchas ben Yair. End of quotation. Both statements are difficult to believe. They did not see Jerusalem Taanit, chapter 3, halakhah 10, which says: they told him to pray for rain, and he said, “Bring in the Passover ovens.” R. Yudan Mari said: this Choni the Circle-Drawer was the grandson of Choni the Circle-Drawer. Near the destruction, the latter went to his workers on the mountain; rain came, he entered a cave, and slept seventy years, until the Temple had been destroyed and built a second time, etc. I subsequently saw in Chiddushei Aggadot that it cites this Jerusalem Talmud account of Choni the Circle-Drawer—that is, Choni who prayed for rain—as having been at the destruction of the First Temple and slept seventy years from its destruction until the Second Temple was built, meaning its construction in 3408. But the Mishnah's event occurred much later, in the time of Shimon ben Shetach, who lived in 3621. Yefeh Mareh writes that there were two men named Choni the Circle-Drawer, and the one in the Mishnah was the other's grandson. Sefer Yuchasin writes in Yosippon's name that Choni was killed outside Jerusalem in the Hasmonean princes' wars. This agrees with our Talmud: because he disappeared from the world for seventy years in sleep, they said he had been killed in the brothers' wars; thus, when he returned, even his grandson did not believe him. End of quotation. In my opinion, one may say that the first Choni slept seventy years until the Second Temple was built, and he was the one who died after praying for death, etc.; the one who prayed for rain was his grandson, killed in the brothers' wars, around 3688. Yet the wording of the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds cannot be made to fit and agree. See Sefer HaGilgulim, letter chet: Choni the Circle-Drawer is Gideon. Because he made an ephod, even though he intended it for Heaven's sake, Israel nevertheless strayed after it; he therefore died during his lifetime, for he slept seventy years, and sleep is one-sixtieth of death. He later asked to die, since Choni was a spark of Elijah, who asked to die, and also a spark of Mordekhai. See there, letter pe: they brought him a thanksgiving bull, and he laid his hand on it, as in Taanit 23a. This alluded to Ahab, reincarnated in that bull, while Choni was Elijah. Ahab corrupted things by his sin and caused great damage; nevertheless, something good was found in him, “because Ahab humbled himself.” On another occasion he pursued Elijah. Therefore Choni, who was Elijah, said, “Bring it to me by force”: formerly he had not followed Elijah, and “I will repair him, because he humbled himself.” He thus said “a bull of acknowledgment,” meaning that on a previous occasion, when he was Ahab, he acknowledged; now “I will repair him through this bull.” It further writes that Gideon, Choni the Circle-Drawer, and Elijah are one spark, and these three effected repairs through bulls: Gideon repaired Shechem through a bull (see there); Elijah offered bulls and repaired Datan and Aviram; Choni repaired Ahab. End of quotation. Gelilot Eretz Yisrael writes that outside Kefar Paniam is a cave where Choni and his wife are buried, with his study house nearby. On the other side is a cave where Abba Chilkiyah, Chanan the Hidden, and R. Yehudah bar Ilai and his seventy students are buried. Elsewhere it writes that R. Yehudah bar Ilai is buried at Ein Zetim. Benjamin's Travels writes that Choni the Circle-Drawer is buried at Kedesh Naphtali. See R. Elazar ben Arakh.
